Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers, and let $h>0$ be a fixed
sampling interval. A real **discrete linear input-state-output experiment** of
state dimension $d$, input dimension $m$, output dimension $p$, and horizon
$q$ consists of matrices $A\in M_{d\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
$B\in M_{d\times m}(\mathbb R)$, and $C\in M_{p\times d}(\mathbb R)$, an
initial state $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and known inputs
$(u_k)_{0\le k<q-1}$ in $\mathbb R^m$. The states are defined by
$$x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k\qquad(0\le k<q-1),$$
and the exact sampled outputs at times $kh$ are $y_k=Cx_k$ for
$0\le k<q$. When observations are perturbed, the observed outputs are
$\widetilde y_k=y_k+\eta_k$ for deterministic error vectors
$\eta_k\in\mathbb R^p$; the exact-data convention is $\eta_k=0$ for all $k$.
No probability law is assigned to the errors. A numerical or discretization
error that changes the forward map is distinct from this additive observation
error.

For an impulse-response experiment with zero initial state, first input
$u_0=v\in\mathbb R^m$, and later inputs zero, the **Markov parameters** are
$$M_k:=CA^kB\in M_{p\times m}(\mathbb R)\qquad(k\ge0),$$
so the output one sample after the impulse is $y_{k+1}=M_kv$. Matrix powers
use $A^0=I_d$ and $A^{k+1}=A^kA$. If $d=0$, the state space consists of its
single zero vector and the matrices have the corresponding empty shapes.

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over
entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication.
Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes,

$$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$

$$(A+A')B=AB+A'B,\qquad A(B+B')=AB+AB',$$

$$0B=0=A0,\qquad (\lambda A)B=\lambda(AB)=A(\lambda B).$$

These identities include every zero-sized shape.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map whose domain $V$ is finite-dimensional over
$F$. Its **nullity** and **rank** are

$$\operatorname{nullity}T:=\dim_F(\ker T),\qquad \operatorname{rank}T:=\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Both dimensions are defined. The kernel is a linear subspace of the
finite-dimensional space $V$, so it is finite-dimensional by
[[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] and
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]. The image is finite-dimensional because
[[lem-kernel-basis-extension-gives-image-basis]] constructs a finite basis of
it from a basis of $V$. Thus rank and nullity are natural numbers, including
when $V$ is the zero space.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Then $\operatorname{rank} T$ equals the number of positive
singular values of $T$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of

In orthonormal bases, the matrix of the adjoint is the conjugate transpose of the matrix.

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $A^+$ as the solution of the four Penrose equations.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have full column rank $n$. Then $A^*A$ is
invertible and

$$A^+=(A^*A)^{-1}A^*.$$

Let $A$ be a finite real or complex matrix. Then $AA^+$ is the orthogonal
projection onto $\operatorname{im}A$, and $A^+A$ is the orthogonal projection
onto $\operatorname{im}A^*$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and let $b\in\mathbb F^m$. Then $A^+b$ is
a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, and among all least-squares solutions it
is the unique one of minimum Euclidean norm.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

derivations.claim: For each $0\le k<q$, the recurrence gives $x_k=A^kx_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}A^{k-1-j}Bu_j$, with the sum empty at $k=0$. At $k=0$ this is $x_0=A^0x_0$. If it holds at $k<q-1$, substitution into $x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k$ and the power recursion give the formula at $k+1$, using associativity and distributivity from [F2]. Multiplying by $C$ and subtracting $f_k$ gives $y_k-f_k=CA^kx_0$, so stacking yields $z=O_qx_0$.

Suppose $d\ge1$ and $O_q$ has full column rank. By [F5] and [F6], an SVD has exactly $d$ positive singular values $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_d=\sigma_{\min}(O_q)>0$. Writing $w$ in the right singular basis gives $\|O_qw\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d s_j^2|w_j|^2\ge\sigma_{\min}(O_q)^2\|w\|_2^2$.

Two states $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$ produce the same corrected stack exactly when $O_q(x-x')=0$. Thus injectivity is equivalent to $\ker O_q=\{0\}$. By [F3] and [F4], this is equivalent to $\operatorname{rank}O_q=d$. When $d=0$, the map has a singleton domain and the empty matrix has rank zero, so the same equivalence holds.

By [F7] and [F8], $O_q^+$ is the unique Moore--Penrose inverse. Set $\widehat x_0=O_q^+(z+e)$; [F11] identifies it as the minimum-norm least-squares estimate, and [F9] with $z=O_qx_0$ gives $w:=\widehat x_0-x_0=O_q^+e$. Hence $O_qw=O_qO_q^+e$. By [F10], this is an orthogonal projection of $e$; the decomposition $e=O_qO_q^+e+(e-O_qO_q^+e)$ has orthogonal summands, so [F12] gives $\|O_qw\|_2\le\|e\|_2$.

Combining steps 1.2 and 2.2 gives $\sigma_{\min}(O_q)\|\widehat x_0-x_0\|_2\le\|O_q(\widehat x_0-x_0)\|_2\le\|e\|_2$. Division by the positive singular value proves the claimed sensitivity bound; step 2.1 proves the injectivity assertion.

Markov matrices
$$M_0,\ldots,M_{2q-1}\in M_{p\times m}(\mathbb R).$$
Use the exact-real linear-algebra model: an exact rank test returns the rank of
a finite real matrix; a thin rank-$d$ singular-value decomposition of a
rank-$d$ matrix $H_0$ returns $H_0=U_d\Sigma_dV_d^{\mathsf T}$ with
$\Sigma_d$ diagonal and strictly positive, and an exact Moore--Penrose routine
returns a matrix satisfying the four Penrose equations. A routine failure or a
returned object that fails its stated exact identities is reported explicitly.
This specification makes no finite-bit computability or complexity claim for
arbitrary real inputs.

Form the $q$-by-$q$ block Hankel matrices
$$H_0=[M_{i+j}]_{0\le i,j<q},\qquad H_1=[M_{i+j+1}]_{0\le i,j<q},$$
each of shape $qp$ by $qm$. Execute the following steps.

1. Apply the exact rank test to $H_0$. If it fails, return
   `failed-solve`; if its value is not $d$, return `inconsistent-rank-data`.

2. If $d=0$, use the empty factorization $H_0=\widehat O\widehat R$ with
   $\widehat O$ of shape $qp$ by $0$ and $\widehat R$ of shape $0$ by $qm$.
   If $d>0$, obtain the thin rank-$d$ SVD in the declared exact model and set
   $$\widehat O:=U_d\Sigma_d^{1/2},\qquad \widehat R:=\Sigma_d^{1/2}V_d^{\mathsf T}.$$
   Verify $H_0=\widehat O\widehat R$, $\operatorname{rank}\widehat O=d$,
   and $\operatorname{rank}\widehat R=d$; if any operation or verification
   fails, return `failed-solve`.

3. Compute the exact Moore--Penrose inverses $\widehat O^+$ and
   $\widehat R^+$ and verify their four Penrose equations. If a computation or
   verification fails, return `failed-solve`.

4. Set $\widehat A:=\widehat O^+H_1\widehat R^+$, let $\widehat B$ be the first $m$ columns of $\widehat R$, and let $\widehat C$ be the first $p$ rows of $\widehat O$. Return `success` with $(\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat C)$. For $d=0$,
   these are the corresponding empty matrices.

The routine can report `failed-solve` for a failed or invalid exact-operation
backend. The existence theorems for finite-matrix SVDs and Moore--Penrose
inverses ensure that the exact mathematical operations requested in steps 2–3
exist; this definition alone asserts no noisy rank selection or stable
parameter recovery.

Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers. Suppose a noiseless
experiment has matrices $A\in M_{d\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
$B\in M_{d\times m}(\mathbb R)$, and $C\in M_{p\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
initial state $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and common inputs
$(u_k)_{0\le k<q-1}$. For any invertible $T\in M_d(\mathbb R)$ define
$$\widehat A=T^{-1}AT,\qquad \widehat B=T^{-1}B,\qquad \widehat C=CT,\qquad \widehat x_0=T^{-1}x_0.$$
The experiment with $(\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat C,\widehat x_0)$ and the
same inputs has the same output $y_k$ at every sample $0\le k<q$. The equality
holds for every horizon and every common input sequence.

derivations.claim: If $d=0$, then $B$ has no rows and $C$ has no columns, so $M_k=0$ for every $k$ and $H_0=H_1=0$. Its rank is zero, and the algorithm's exact empty factorization and empty pseudoinverses return the unique empty matrices. Taking $T=I_0$ gives the asserted similarity. Henceforth suppose $d\ge1$.

For $0\le i,j<q$, the $(i,j)$ block of $H_0$ is $M_{i+j}=CA^{i+j}B=(CA^i)(A^jB)$ by [F1] and [F2], and the corresponding block of $H_1$ is $M_{i+j+1}=(CA^i)A(A^jB)$. Thus $H_0=O_qR_q$ and $H_1=O_qAR_q$. Because $R_q$ has rank $d$ and codomain $\mathbb R^d$, it is surjective; because $O_q$ has rank $d$ and domain $\mathbb R^d$, it is injective. Therefore $\operatorname{im}H_0=\operatorname{im}O_q$ and $\operatorname{rank}H_0=d$.

The exact rank test in the algorithm therefore returns $d$. The SVD factorization and pseudoinverses exist by [F6], and the stated successful-call hypothesis ensures that the algorithm returns factors $H_0=\widehat O\widehat R$ with each factor of rank $d$ and returns `success`. In particular $\widehat R$ is surjective, so $\operatorname{im}H_0=\operatorname{im}\widehat O$. Combining this with step 1.2 gives $\operatorname{im}\widehat O=\operatorname{im}O_q$.

The columns of $O_q$ and $\widehat O$ are bases of the same $d$-dimensional image by step 2.1. Thus there is a unique $d\times d$ matrix $T$ with $\widehat O=O_qT$. If $Tv=0$, then $\widehat Ov=O_qTv=0$; since $\widehat O$ has rank $d$, its kernel is zero, so $v=0$. Rank-nullity [F3] and [F4] makes the square matrix $T$ surjective as well as injective; hence $T$ is invertible by [F8]. From $O_qR_q=H_0=O_qT\widehat R$ and injectivity of $O_q$, $R_q=T\widehat R$, so $\widehat R=T^{-1}R_q$.

Substituting $O_q=\widehat O T^{-1}$ and $R_q=T\widehat R$ into the identity in step 1.2 gives $H_1=\widehat O(T^{-1}AT)\widehat R$. Since $\widehat O$ has full column rank, $\widehat O^+\widehat O=I_d$: the equation $\widehat O\widehat O^+\widehat O=\widehat O$ from [F7] and injectivity imply this identity. Since $\widehat R$ has full row rank, $\widehat R\widehat R^+=I_d$: [F7] gives $\widehat R\widehat R^+\widehat R=\widehat R$, and surjectivity implies the identity. The algorithm's formula then yields $\widehat A=\widehat O^+H_1\widehat R^+=T^{-1}AT$.

The first $m$ columns of $R_q$ form $B$, and the first $p$ rows of $O_q$ form $C$. Taking those blocks in $\widehat R=T^{-1}R_q$ and $\widehat O=O_qT$ gives $\widehat B=T^{-1}B$ and $\widehat C=CT$. Hence the triple returned by the algorithm satisfies all three similarity identities.

By [F9], the similarity identities imply identical outputs for every finite common-input experiment when initial states are related by $T^{-1}$. With zero initial state and an impulse input, this gives $\widehat C\widehat A^k\widehat B=CA^kB$ for every $k\ge0$. This is exact realization modulo state similarity; it asserts no stability under perturbed Markov data.

\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ (Finite sums and finite products, by recursion). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ (Integer powers $a^m$), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, let
$A:X\to Y$ be a compact linear forward map (the closure of $A(B)$ is compact
in $Y$ for every bounded set $B\subseteq X$), and let $A_h:X\to Y$ be a
bounded linear discretized map with finite-dimensional range. For a datum
$b\in Y$, let $\lambda>0$ be the coefficient of $\|x\|_X^2$ in the Tikhonov
objective $\|Ax-b\|_Y^2+\lambda\|x\|_X^2$. Supply adjoints $A^*:Y\to X$ and
$A_h^*:Y\to X$ satisfying
$\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X$ and
$\langle A_hx,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A_h^*y\rangle_X$, where the inner products
are linear in their first arguments. Assume the shifted normal operators
$A^*A+\lambda I_X$ and $A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X$ are bijective, and define
$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A_h^*.$$

For a truth $x^\dagger\in X$, data perturbation $e\in Y$, and $\delta\ge0$
with $\|e\|\le\delta$, put
$$y=Ax^\dagger,\qquad y_\delta=y+e,\qquad y_{h,\delta}=A_hx^\dagger+e,\qquad d_h=(A-A_h)x^\dagger=y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}.$$
For any returned output $\widetilde x_h\in X$, define its exact discrete
normal-equation residual by
$$r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x_h-A_h^*y_{h,\delta}.$$
The five-channel error budget is the ordered tuple
$(b_{\mathrm{bias}},b_{\mathrm{data}},b_{\mathrm{operator}},b_{\mathrm{pre}},b_{\mathrm{solve}})$, where
$$\begin{aligned}b_{\mathrm{bias}}&=x^\dagger-R_\lambda y,\qquad b_{\mathrm{data}}=R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta,\\b_{\mathrm{operator}}&=(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_{h,\delta},\qquad b_{\mathrm{pre}}=R_\lambda d_h,\\b_{\mathrm{solve}}&=R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h.\end{aligned}$$
The five entries are, in order, the truth-bias, data-perturbation,
regularized-operator, pre-inversion, and algebraic-solve error vectors.
The scalar total budget is the sum of the five channel norms. The raw
pre-inversion forward residual is $d_h$; its reconstruction contribution is
$b_{\mathrm{pre}}$. The operator channel measures the difference between the
regularized exact and discretized operators. The solve channel measures the
returned output's difference from the exact discrete Tikhonov output. The
definition supplies no rate or arithmetic residual certificate.
